findings.location: Section 4B 'What models of actual continuation find' — the sentence beginning 'Four designs model persistence rather than feeling, and none finds income level operative' and the Zhao clause 'Superchat income shows no significant main effect (β=−0.136, p=0.111)'
findings.issue: The draft reports Zhao's null main effect for income and silently drops the same model's significant income-by-time interaction, which the depth investigator recorded as evidence that income's protective effect is real but small and cumulative — so the categorical claim 'none finds income level operative' is contradicted by the pipeline's own reading of its lead source.
findings.evidence: [[interim-report-quit-driver-money-vs-motivation]] line 60: 'Total Superchat Income's main effect on hazard is *not* statistically significant (β=−0.136, p=0.111) — but its interaction with time is (p=0.010), meaning income's protective effect is small and only accumulates gradually.' Same note: Zhao's income variable is Superchat only, and [[who-reaps-all-the-superchats-a-large-scale-analysis-of-income]] itself states 'publicly observable tipping and membership revenue understates top-creator income because Hololive's own financial reporting shows merchandising overtook Superchats and memberships as the leading revenue stream after 2022.'
findings.recommendation: Add the significant income-by-time interaction (p=0.010) alongside the null main effect, and downgrade 'none finds income level operative' to something like 'none finds income level a strong or immediate predictor.' Add a clause noting Zhao's income variable is Superchat revenue only and that the authors themselves say it understates total creator income — so the model tests one revenue stream, not income. Optionally in the same paragraph, note that the Adpocalypse panel's 'affected population growing rather than shrinking' is measured on Patreon accounts and by construction cannot observe creators who left without a Patreon page.

findings.location: Opening summary ('Reasons for quitting have never been elicited from anyone who quit') and Section 4 opener ('Every instrument here does the opposite') and Section 4C ('The closest exit-reason elicitation anywhere samples the wrong side of the transaction')
findings.issue: The corpus contains named, dated, creator-side statements of why creators quit — the 2023 Bilibili 停更 wave — and the draft omits them entirely, so its universal absence claim is stated more strongly than the vault supports, and the omitted evidence happens to cut toward income insufficiency, against Section 4B's conclusion.
findings.evidence: [[stop-updating-a-textual-analysis-of-chinese-viewers]]: a 1.029m-follower Bilibili creator announced on 12 Jan 2023 stopping because 'unable to make ends meet financially'; a 3.833m-follower creator announced on 31 Mar 2023 that creating on Bilibili was 'not profitable, even leading to losses,' with fatigue secondary; '#Vloggers are quitting Bilibili' ranked #1 on Sina Weibo Hot Search on 2 Apr 2023 with 420m same-day views; n=1,176 viewer comments coded Aug 2023. Flagged for inclusion in comparisons.md, 'Tension 2 revision' ('the closest non-English equivalents that exist').
findings.recommendation: Insert two or three sentences in Section 4C reporting the Bilibili exodus with its dates, follower counts and the n=1,176 comment analysis, labelled accurately as public self-announcements by individual named creators plus viewer-perception coding, not a sampled exit survey. Then narrow the absence claims in the lede and Section 4 opener from 'never elicited from anyone who quit' to the defensible form: no instrument has ever put the question to a *sample* of departed creators. Note that this evidence points at income insufficiency, and say so where Section 4B concludes.

findings.location: Section 2B, the paragraph beginning 'These rows must not be averaged, ranged or ranked' and the permitted headline sentence 'across four telemetry and complete-record datasets ... under 2% of everyone who registered an account or held a channel'
findings.issue: The draft privileges the full-population denominator without ever stating the strongest case for the survey denominator — that an occupational question is about people who practise the occupation, which is exactly the denominator the draft's own ACS and BLS rows use — and so dismisses the survey regime by scope arithmetic rather than engaging it.
findings.evidence: [[interim-report-living-wage-share-magnitude]]: 'Survey-based figures in the 4-63% range (Linktree, NeoReach, Goldman, TikTok Indonesia) are not wrong on their own terms, but they answer a narrower question.' The on-its-own-terms rebuttal is also in the vault: [[pdf-linktree-creatorreport-2022-02f3aa05a27be6fecb3537b13d5ec9depdf]] — 46% of self-identified full-time creators earned under $1,000/year, i.e. 'full-time' is a self-description, not an income-verified category. Draft's own rows [[artists-and-other-cultural-workers]] and [[independent-artists-writers-and-performers-may-2022-oews-industry-specific-occup]] use primary-occupation and payroll denominators.
findings.recommendation: Insert two sentences before or after the permitted headline sentence: first granting that the survey denominator answers a legitimate and arguably more occupational question, and noting that official occupational statistics (ACS primary occupation, BLS payroll) use exactly that narrower denominator; then rebutting it on its own terms with Linktree's internal finding that 46% of self-identified full-timers earn under $1,000/year, so the self-identification gate does not screen for income. This converts a scope dismissal into an engagement.

findings.location: Section 2C heading 'Two measured biases that push in opposite directions' and the closing clause of the Section 2B headline sentence, 'with both bias directions known and unquantified'
findings.issue: The draft never states which way each bias moves the sub-2% number, and its argument is asymmetric: it supplies a labelled inference bounding the correction that would raise the figure via the denominator, while leaving the off-platform-income correction — the corpus's larger candidate — unquantified even though a conditional magnitude was recorded.
findings.evidence: comparisons.md 'Tension 1 revision': 'If the music ratio generalises, the correction is 5–7x'; [[music-creators-earnings-in]] audio streaming 6% / all digital 14% / live 31% of average UK music creator income (n=708, 2019). Also unused: [[rich-get-richer-platform-attention-and-earnings-inequality]] — 'Patreon crowdfunding links appear in only 2.55% of YouTube video descriptions versus 49% for cross-platform links, so Patreon-based earnings measures capture a small and selected slice of total creator income,' which matters because three of the draft's living-wage rows are Patreon.
findings.recommendation: State explicitly, in one sentence, the direction each bias moves the sub-2% headline. Add the conditional magnitude ('if the UK music platform-to-total ratio generalised, the correction would be roughly five- to sevenfold') immediately followed by the draft's existing caveat that no individual-level platform-to-total ratio exists for YouTube, Twitch or Patreon. Also correct 'both bias directions known and unquantified' — the draft does bound the registration-denominator one. Optionally add the 2.55%-versus-49% link-prevalence datapoint as a second reason Patreon-derived shares are a selected slice.

findings.location: Section 1B 'The absence, and who holds the missing data' — the sentence 'Investor filings were checked; Spotify's tier retention above is the only hit'
findings.issue: The report's most consequential absence claim is asserted at high confidence with a one-clause search record that names neither the filings checked nor the databases and languages searched, and it drops the depth investigator's explicit caveat that the searches were English-only.
findings.evidence: [[interim-report-attrition-telemetry-absence]] lines 68–77: 'five independent search angles (three prior OpenAlex sweeps, plus my own academic-API searches and TubeCensus's own literature review)'; four language/platform angles (Wikipedia, OSS, Bilibili/Douyin, AfreecaTV/SOOP); and the standing caveat 'my English-only academic-API queries (Semantic Scholar rate-limited throughout this session)... suggestive of absence but not conclusive given the language barrier in indexing.' comparisons.md 'Tension 2 revision' names the filings: Bilibili 20-F, Kuaishou HK prospectus, Roblox S-1/10-K, Patreon State of Create, Spotify Loud & Clear.
findings.recommendation: Expand the search-record sentence to name the specific disclosure channels checked (Bilibili's 20-F, Kuaishou's Hong Kong prospectus, Roblox's S-1 and 10-K, Patreon's State of Create, Spotify's Loud & Clear) and the academic channels (three OpenAlex sweeps plus targeted academic-API searches across Wikipedia, open-source, Bilibili/Douyin and AfreecaTV/SOOP literatures). Add one clause carrying the language limitation: the academic queries were English-language and Semantic Scholar was rate-limited, so a Chinese- or Korean-language cohort-survival paper cannot be ruled out. Also worth one clause: the two best-identified income-shock natural experiments in the adjacent gig literature (a Lyft transparency rollout, 47m rides [[platform-design-earnings-transparency-and]]) measure hours, not exit.

findings.location: Section 1C 'Documented analogues' — 'Two literatures on unpaid contributors have the methodology this field lacks'
findings.issue: The corpus contains a paid-platform cohort survival curve that the draft omits, which both undercuts the 'unpaid contributors only' framing and supplies the closest genuine methodological analogue with a monetary incentive present.
findings.evidence: [[an-analysis-of-the-labor-market-for-ubers-driver-partners-in-the]] (Hall & Krueger): among 11,267 US UberBLACK/uberX driver-partners first driving Jan–Jun 2013 with at least four trips, 11% became inactive (no trip for 6+ months) within one month, 70% remained active at six months, more than 50% at one year. Same note documents the conflict of interest: Hall was an Uber employee and shareholder, Krueger a paid Uber consultant, and Berg & Johnston 2019 (ILR Review) argue this produced selective framing.
findings.recommendation: Add a short passage to Section 1C giving the Hall & Krueger cohort curve with its n, cohort window and definition of inactivity, immediately followed by the authorship conflict of interest and the Berg & Johnston critique. Adjust the framing sentence so it no longer claims only unpaid-contributor literatures have this methodology — the honest statement is that the paid analogue exists but sits in ride-hailing, not content, and carries a sponsor-authorship problem.

findings.location: Section 2 as a whole — Section 2B's line naming 'dimensionless shape statistics — mean/median ratios, Gini, Pareto alpha ... hazard ratios' as one of only two surviving comparison classes
findings.issue: The draft names shape statistics and within-instrument time series as the only two defensible comparison classes and then presents almost none of them: the corpus's concentration-trend literature — three independent groups, three platforms, two inequality statistics — is absent, as is the counter-position inside it, and Houssard's elite-tier stability sits unreconciled in the attrition table.
findings.evidence: [[quantifying-the-creator-economy-a-large-scale-analysis-of-patreon]] (Patreon within-topic Gini 0.30→0.60, 2015–2020); [[who-reaps-all-the-superchats-a-large-scale-analysis-of-income]] (VTuber between-creator Gini 0.60→0.75, 2018–2023); [[rich-get-richer-platform-attention-and-earnings-inequality]] (Pareto alpha ≈2.0 falling on YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and Twitch 2018–2024, n=104,719 official Patreon data; winner-take-all regime beginning at $26–70/month). Counter-cut in the same corpus: 'every earnings decile grew in absolute terms from 2013 to 2020 and smaller creators show higher relative audience growth, which cuts against a pure winner-take-all reading.' Reconciliation pre-committed in source-tensions.json, 'Concentration worsening versus elite-tier stability': Houssard [[vol0123456789-2]] measures churn *within* the elite tier, the others measure the distribution *across* the population — compatible, not contradictory.
findings.recommendation: Add a short paragraph (roughly four sentences) to Section 2 presenting the concentration time series with sample sizes and windows, stating the resolution that Houssard's elite-tier flux and the widening distribution are compatible because they measure different things, and carrying the counter-finding that every Patreon earnings decile grew in absolute terms. This is the one comparison class the draft itself licenses and then does not use; flagging as borderline structural since it needs a new paragraph rather than a qualifier.

findings.location: Section 6C 'Two provenance chains, one standard' — 'Applying one standard gives an asymmetric result: the Southeast Asian chain has a survey underneath it and the Western chain does not'
findings.issue: The asymmetry conclusion is drawn from a single traced pairing that compares unlike quantities — a Western population headcount against a Southeast Asian income share — and the draft never states that the comparison is quantity-specific, leaving a reader free to generalise it into 'Western evidence is worse,' which the rest of the report contradicts.
findings.evidence: The draft's own table labels the columns 'Western population chain' and 'Southeast Asian income chain.' Against a general reading: the Western income record includes complete-record and telemetry instruments with no SEA equivalent — [[vol0123456789-3]] (139,366 Patreon campaigns), [[httpsdoiorg10117720563051231180628]] (~36.1m channels), [[twitch-streamer-earnings-increase-for-top-gamers-data-from-hack-shows-wsj]] — while the SEA record in Section 5D is mostly documented absences plus a fabricated Indonesian journal article [[pengaruh-ekonomi-kreator-digital-terhadap-pendapatan-generasi-z-di-perkotaan-stu]].
findings.recommendation: Add one qualifying sentence after the asymmetry conclusion, scoping it to the quantity actually traced: the Western *population count* is in worse provenance shape than the Indonesian *income share*, and this does not generalise to the two evidence bases, since Western income measurement has complete-record and telemetry instruments that Southeast Asia has none of. Keep the one-standard point — it survives the qualifier and is sharper for it.

findings.location: Section 2A, the paragraph beginning 'Four constraints travel with the October 2021 Twitch leak'
findings.issue: The draft carries the leak's four scope constraints but drops the provenance dispute entirely — the data is unconfirmed by Twitch, streamers gave mixed confirmations of their own figures, and the tables are internally inconsistent — while also omitting the verification that cuts the other way, so a reader gets neither side of a live disagreement about a dataset the report uses for its flagship 'median under $28.'
findings.evidence: [[twitch-responds-to-leak-revealing-earnings-of-top-streamers-and-more-dexerto]] — streamers gave mixed responses when asked to confirm their own figures; leaked tables inconsistent with each other, e.g. Asmongold's September 2021 monthly figure extrapolating to $3.4m against a $2.55m cumulative listing. Countervailing: [[twitch-streamer-earnings-increase-for-top-gamers-data-from-hack-shows-wsj]] cross-checked one streamer's pay stubs against the leak and matched to within 25 cents. Pre-committed as tension 'The Twitch leak: best available measurement versus unverified breach data.'
findings.recommendation: Insert one sentence adding a fifth constraint: the dataset is unverified breach data that Twitch has never confirmed, individual streamers have both confirmed and denied their own entries, and at least one internal inconsistency is documented — balanced in the same sentence by the WSJ pay-stub match to within 25 cents, which is why the report uses it anyway.

findings.location: Section 2B living-wage matrix, the adjacent 12% (Linktree) and 43% (NeoReach) rows and the paragraph following the matrix
findings.issue: The corpus's cleanest natural experiment on vendor-survey bias — two surveys, same year, same $50,000 threshold, answers 3.5x apart, differing only in recruitment channel — is left as two undifferentiated table rows, so the report gains a matrix row where it could have gained a measurement of the recruitment effect.
findings.evidence: source-tensions.json, 'NeoReach versus Linktree: same year, same question, 3.5x apart': NeoReach's respondent pool is an influencer-agency roster in which 4% of respondents have over 10 million followers, and no methodology statement for it exists anywhere in the corpus [[creator-earnings-breakdown-the-creator-economy-today]]; Linktree n=9,576, ~95% completion, fielded 2021, creator defined by intent [[pdf-linktree-creatorreport-2022-02f3aa05a27be6fecb3537b13d5ec9depdf]]. The pre-committed resolution says to present the pair as the demonstration and to cite NeoReach only as that illustration.
findings.recommendation: Add one or two sentences after the matrix drawing the pair explicitly: same year, same threshold, 3.5x apart, the only material difference being who was invited to respond, so the gap is a measurement of the recruitment effect rather than a disagreement about the world. Note that NeoReach discloses no sample size, fielding date or country anywhere and that 4% of its respondents have over 10 million followers, and state that its 43% is retained only as that illustration.

findings.location: Section 3, the paragraph beginning 'Three independent measurements find output volume and threshold-crossing, not elapsed tenure, to be operative'
findings.issue: The tenure-is-not-operative reframe is asserted from three within-content measurements without acknowledging the one adjacent-platform result in the corpus that finds a real tenure effect on earnings.
findings.evidence: [[an-analysis-of-the-labor-market-for-ubers-driver-partners-in-the]]: 'Uber driver-partner earnings-per-hour show a quadratic relationship with tenure on the platform, peaking at approximately 14 months of accumulated seniority' — with the same sponsor-authorship caveat noted above.
findings.recommendation: Add a short qualifying clause noting that in the adjacent paid-platform literature tenure does show a measured earnings gradient (Uber, peak at ~14 months of accumulated seniority, sponsor-authored), so the claim being made is specific to content platforms and to the three measurements cited, not a general result about platform work.

findings.location: Section 6C, 'The 63% rests on a real if thin instrument and is citable with its caveats'
findings.issue: The verdict sentence a reader is most likely to lift does not restate the caveat that most limits it — that the denominator behind the 63% is undisclosed — so the figure travels out of the report lighter than it entered.
findings.evidence: [[the-tiktok-effect]] and [[tiktoks-socio-economic-impact-in-southeast-asia-a-summary-of-the-report-kadence]]: the sub-base of 'creators who use TikTok as a source of income' is disclosed for no country except Myanmar (n=26); the survey was commissioned by TikTok and fielded through its own vendor in Aug–Sep 2022 among self-selected active TikTok users. The draft states these in Section 5C but not at the point of the citable verdict.
findings.recommendation: Extend the verdict sentence with the three caveats in compressed inline form: the denominator behind the percentage is undisclosed for Indonesia, the instrument is platform-commissioned among self-selected active users of that platform, and it is now nearly four years old. One clause, not a new paragraph.
